metadata.title: On weight initialization in deep neural networks

nodes.name: Weight variance selection problem
nodes.statement: The problem can be stated as follows: If the weights in a neural network are initialized using samples from a normal distribution, ${\cal{N}}(0,v^{2})$, how should $v^{2}$ be chosen to ensure that the variance of the outputs from the different layers are approximately the same?
nodes.statement_short: Choose the variance $v^2$ of Gaussian weight initialization so that all layer outputs have equal variance.

nodes.name: Glorot-Bengio linear-activation initialization
nodes.statement: The first systematic analysis of this problem was conducted by Glorot and Bengio \cite{glorot2010understanding} who showed that for a linear activation function, the optimal value of $v^{2} = 1/N$, where $N$ is the number of nodes feeding into that layer.
assumptions: where $N$ is the number of nodes feeding into that layer

nodes.name: Xavier initialization
nodes.statement: Although the paper makes several assumptions about the inputs to the model, it works extremely well in many cases and is widely used in the initialization of neural networks to date; this initialization scheme is commonly referred to as the {\it{Xavier initialization}}.

nodes.name: He initialization
nodes.statement: In an important follow up paper, He and colleagues \cite{he2015delving} argue that the {\it{Xavier initialization}} does not work well with the RELU activation function, and instead propose an initialization of $v^{2} = 2/N$ (commonly referred to as the {\it{He initialization}}).

nodes.name: Why He converges but Xavier does not (30-layer RELU network)
nodes.statement: In support of their initialization, they provide an example of a 30 layer neural network which converges with the {\it{He initialization}}, but not under the {\it{Xavier initialization}}. To the best of my knowledge, the precise reason for the convergence of one method and the non-convergence of the other is not fully understood.
nodes.statement_short: Why does the 30-layer RELU network converge under He but not under Xavier initialization?

nodes.name: Deep neural network layer recursions
nodes.statement: Consider a deep neural network with $M$ layers. The relationship between the inputs to the $m^{th}$ layer ($x_{m}$) and $m+1^{th}$ layer ($x_{m+1}$) are described by the recursions \be y_{m}(i) = \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N}{\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)x_{m}(j) = \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N} p_{ij} \enum{in1} \ee and \be x_{m+1}(i) = \mbox{g}(y_{m}(i)). \enum{in2} \ee Here $p_{j} = {\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)x_{m}(j)$, ${\bf{W}}_{m}$ is a matrix of weights for the $m^{th}$ layer, $g$ is the non-linear activation function, and $N$ is the number of nodes in the hidden layers respectively.
nodes.statement_short: Layer recursion $y_m = W_m x_m$, $x_{m+1} = g(y_m)$ with $N$ hidden nodes per layer.

nodes.name: i.i.d. Gaussian weights
nodes.statement: The weights ${\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)$ are assumed to be independent identically distributed normal random variables with mean 0 and variance $v^{2}$.

nodes.name: i.i.d. standardized inputs
nodes.statement: Consistent with the assumptions in \cite{glorot2010understanding} and \cite{he2015delving}, I assume that the inputs to the first layer are independent and identically distributed random variables with mean 0 and variance 1.

nodes.name: Notation $r_m$, $u_m^2$
nodes.statement: For convenience, I use $r_{m}$ and $u_{m}^{2}$ to denote the mean and variance of $y_{m}(i)$ respectively.

nodes.name: Layer input moments $\mu_m$, $s_m^2$
nodes.statement: Due to the symmetry in the problem, all inputs to the $m^{th}$ layer will have the same means and variances during the first forward pass (i.e., $E(x_{m}(i)) = \mu_m$ and $Var(x_{m}(i)) = s_{m}^{2}$ for all $i$); the covariances between the inputs to the $m^{th}$ layer need not be 0.
nodes.statement_short: By symmetry all inputs to layer $m$ share mean $\mu_m$ and variance $s_m^2$ in the first forward pass.

nodes.name: Variance-preserving initialization goal
nodes.statement: The goal is to find the value of $v^{2}$ which ensures that $s_{1}^{2} \approx s_{2}^{2} ...\approx s_{M}^{2} = 1$ during the first forward pass.

nodes.name: Independence of weights and layer inputs
nodes.statement: During the first iteration, $W_{m}(i,j)$ is independent of $x_{m}(k)$ for all values of $i, j$ and $k$
conclusions: $W_{m}(i,j)$ is independent of $x_{m}(k)$ for all values of $i, j$ and $k$

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 1
nodes.statement: Using the recursions in \eref{in1} and \eref{in2}, $x_{m}(k)$ can be expressed as some non-linear function of the weights in the first $m-1$ layers, and the inputs to the first layer. Since the weights in the $m^{th}$ layer are independent of the inputs to the first layer and the weights in all other layers, the weights in the $m^{th}$ layer will also be independent of any non-linear function of these quantities. Therefore, $W_{m}(i,j)$ is independent of $x_{m}(k)$ for all values of $i, j$ and $k$. Furthermore, since $W_{m}(i,j)$ is independent of $x_{m}(k)$ and $x_{m}(l)$, $W_{m}(i,j)$ will also be independent of $x_{m}(k)x_{m}(l)$\qedsymbol
nodes.statement_short: $x_m$ is a function of earlier weights and inputs, so the independent layer-$m$ weights are independent of it.

nodes.name: Zero mean of pre-activations
nodes.statement: Taking expectations in \eref{in1} and using proposition 1, along with the fact that $E({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)) = 0$ yields \be r_{m} = E(y_{m}(i)) = \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N} E({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j))E(x_{m}(j)) = 0. \enum{in201} \ee

nodes.name: Derivation of the pre-activation variance
nodes.statement: Therefore, $u_{m}^{2} = Var(y_{m}(i)) = E\left(y_{m}(i)^{2}\right) - \left(E(y_{m}(i))\right)^{2} = E\left(y_{m}(i)^{2}\right)$. Using \eref{in1}, \be \begin{split} u_{m}^{2} &= E\left(\sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N}{\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)x_{m}(j)\right)^{2} \\ &= \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N} E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)^{2}x_{m}(j)^{2}\right) + 2\sum E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)x_{m}(j){\bf{W}}_{m}(k,l)x_{m}(l)\right). \\ \enum{in203} \end{split} \ee From proposition 1, ${\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)$ and ${\bf{W}}_{m}(k,l)$ will (a) be independent of each other, and (b) be independent of $x_{m}(j)x_{m}(l)$. Using these results, along with the fact that $E({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)) = 0 $ gives \newline \be E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)x_{m}(j){\bf{W}}_{m}(k,l)x_{m}(l)\right) = E({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j))E({\bf{W}}_{m}(k,l))E(x_{m}(j)x_{m}(l)) = 0. \enum{in2041} \ee \newline Plugging \eref{in2041} into \eref{in203} gives
nodes.statement_short: Expand the square; cross terms vanish by independence and zero-mean weights.

nodes.name: Pre-activation variance formula
nodes.statement: \be \begin{split} u_{m}^{2} &= \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N} E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)^{2}x_{m}(j)^{2}\right) \\ &= \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N} E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)^{2}\right)E\left(x_{m}(j)^{2}\right) \\ &= Nv^{2}(s_{m}^{2} + \mu_{m}^{2}) \\ \enum{in204} \end{split} \ee for all $i$. Interestingly, this result holds for any arbitrary covariance structure of the inputs to the $m^{th}$ layer.
conclusions: this result holds for any arbitrary covariance structure of the inputs to the $m^{th}$ layer
nodes.statement_short: $u_m^2 = N v^2 (s_m^2 + \mu_m^2)$ for any input covariance structure.

nodes.name: Large hidden-layer width
nodes.statement: I make the additional assumption that the number of nodes in the hidden layer ($N$) is `large'; this assumption is reasonable given that most neural networks have several hundred nodes in the hidden layers.

nodes.name: Approximate normality of pre-activations
nodes.statement: $y_{m}(i)$ will be approximately normally distributed for all values of $m$ and $i$.
assumptions: the number of nodes in the hidden layer ($N$) is `large'
conclusions: $y_{m}(i)$ will be approximately normally distributed for all values of $m$ and $i$.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 2
nodes.statement: For the first iteration, note that $E(p_{ij}) = E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)x_{m}(j)\right) = E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)\right)E\left(x_{m}(j)\right) = 0$. Furthermore, for $j \neq k$, \be \begin{split} Cov(p_{ij},p_{ik})&= E(p_{ij}p_{ik}) - E(p_{ij})E(p_{ik}) \\ &= E(p_{ij}p_{ik}) \\ &= E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)x_{m}(j){\bf{W}}_{m}(i,k)x_{m}(k)\right) = 0,\\ \end{split} \ee where the last equality follows from \eref{in2041}. This implies that $p_{i1}$, $p_{i2}$ ... $p_{iN}$ are independent and identically distributed random variables. Therefore by the Central Limit Theorem, we expect $y_{m}(i) = \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N} p_{ij}$ to converge to a normal distribution when $N$ is large \cite{lehmann2004elements}. Even when $p_{i1}$, $p_{i2}$ ... $p_{iN}$ are dependent and not identically distributed, the conditions required to ensure that $y_{m}(i) = \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N} p_{ij}$ converges to a normal distribution are weak (for a list of all the conditions, see Theorem 2.8.2 in \cite{lehmann2004elements}). Thus, $y_{m}(i)$ is expected to to be approximately normally distributed during most iterations. \qedsymbol
nodes.statement_short: Summands $p_{ij}$ are zero-mean and uncorrelated; apply the Central Limit Theorem for large $N$.

nodes.name: First-order Taylor approximation of the activation
nodes.statement: When $g(x)$ is differentiable at 0, we can perform a Taylor expansion in \eref{in2} about $E(y_{m}(i)) = 0$. Assuming that the higher order terms can be ignored, \be x_{m+1}(i) \approx g(0) + (y_{m} - 0)g'(0). \enum{in205} \ee
nodes.statement_short: Linearize $g$ at 0, ignoring higher-order terms.

nodes.name: Derivation of the layer moment recursions (differentiable case)
nodes.statement: Taking the expectation in \eref{in205} gives \be \mu_{m+1} = E(x_{m+1}(i)) \approx g(0). \enum{in206} \ee This equation suggests that the expected value of the inputs to the $(m+1)^{th}$ layer has little dependence on the moments of the inputs to the ${m}^{th}$ layer. Using this result recursively suggests that for all layers (barring the first), \be \mu_{j} = g(0) \mbox{ for all } j\geq 1 \enum{in2061}. \ee Using \eref{in204} and \eref{in2061}, the variance of $x_{m+1}(i)$ can be computed from \eref{in205} as \be \begin{split} s_{m+1}^{2} = Var(x_{m+1}(i)) &\approx (g'(0))^{2} Var(y_{m}(i)) \\ &= N(g'(0))^{2}v^{2}(s_{m}^{2} + \mu_{m}^{2}) \\ &= N(g'(0))^{2}v^{2}(s_{m}^{2} + g(0)^{2}) . \enum{in207} \end{split} \ee
nodes.statement_short: Take mean and variance of the linearized activation and substitute the pre-activation variance formula.

nodes.name: General weight initialization for activations differentiable at 0
nodes.statement: Using the condition $s_{m}^{2} \approx s_{m-1}^{2} ... = s_{1}^{2} = 1$ along with \eref{in2061} and \eref{in207} gives \be v^{2} = \frac{1}{N(g'(0))^{2}(1+g(0)^{2})}, \enum{in208} \ee \noindent Equation \eref{in208} provide a general weight initialization strategy for any arbitrary differentiable activation function.
assumptions: Assuming that the higher order terms can be ignored
nodes.statement_short: Variance-preserving initialization $v^2 = 1/(N g'(0)^2 (1+g(0)^2))$ for any activation differentiable at 0.

nodes.name: Backward-pass constraint not required
nodes.statement: In their calculations, \cite{glorot2010understanding} and \cite{he2015delving} impose an additional set of constraints to ensure that the variance is maintained even during the backward pass. I believe that this is not required, since the requirement that the variance of the inputs at each layer be the same ensures that the gradient flows through in the backward pass.

nodes.name: Xavier initialization for hyperbolic tangent
nodes.statement: For the hyperbolic tangent \be g(x) =\mbox{tanh}(x), \ee we have $g(0) = 0$ and $g'(0) = 1$. Plugging these results in \eref{in208} yields \be v \approx \frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}, \enum{tanh1} \ee which is precisely the {\it{Xavier Initialization}}.
nodes.statement_short: For tanh, the general formula gives $v \approx 1/\sqrt{N}$, the Xavier initialization.

nodes.name: Sequential saturation with tanh (Glorot-Bengio question)
nodes.statement: In their analysis of a neural network with the hyperbolic tangent activations, \cite{glorot2010understanding} find that the deeper layers in the neural network have a greater proportion of unsaturated nodes than the shallower layers. As is stated in their paper, `why this is happening remains to be understood'.
nodes.section: Sequential saturation with the hyperbolic tangent
nodes.statement_short: Why do deeper tanh layers have fewer saturated units than shallower ones?

nodes.name: Explanation of sequential saturation
nodes.statement: To explain their finding, I begin by noting that in \cite{glorot2010understanding}, the authors initialize the weights using samples from a uniform distribution $\left(U[-1/\sqrt{N},1/\sqrt{N}]\right)$ having a variance of $1/3N$. Therefore, from \eref{in2061} and \eref{in207}, with $g(0) = 0$ and $g'(0) = 1$, we have $\mu_{m} = 0$ and \be s_{m+1}^{2} = \frac{1}{3}s_{m}^{2} < s_{m}^{2} \ee \enum{seq1} respectively. From \eref{in204}, this implies that $u_{m+1}^{2}<u_{m}^{2}$ for all $m$ (i.e., $u_{m}^{2}$ is a decreasing function of $m$). Furthermore from proposition 2, $y_{m}(i) \sim {\cal{N}}(0,u_{m}^{2})$. Therefore, $x_{m+1}(i)$ will be the tanh transformation of a normal random variable. Using results from \cite{godfrey2009tanh}, $x_{m+1}(i) = \mbox{tanh}(y_{m}(i))$ will have a probability density function (pdf) given by \be f(y) = \frac{1}{1-y^{2}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi u_{m}^{2}}}\mbox{e}^{\left({-\frac{t_{y}^{2}}{2u_{m}^{2}}}\right)} \enum{tanh1}, \ee where \be t_{y} = \frac{1}{2} ln\left(\frac{1+y}{1-y}\right). \ee Plots of this pdf for different values of $u_{m}$ (provided in Figure \ref{fig:tanh}) produce trends similar to those observed by the simulation studies of \cite{glorot2010understanding} (figure 4 in their paper). A comparison of Figure \ref{fig:tanh} and figure 4 of \cite{glorot2010understanding} suggests that $u_{m}^{2}$ is a decreasing function of $m$, as is expected.
nodes.section: Sequential saturation with the hyperbolic tangent
nodes.statement_short: Uniform init of variance $1/3N$ makes $u_m^2$ shrink with depth; tanh of a Gaussian is bimodal for large $u_m$.

nodes.name: Density of tanh of a Gaussian
nodes.statement: Using results from \cite{godfrey2009tanh}, $x_{m+1}(i) = \mbox{tanh}(y_{m}(i))$ will have a probability density function (pdf) given by \be f(y) = \frac{1}{1-y^{2}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi u_{m}^{2}}}\mbox{e}^{\left({-\frac{t_{y}^{2}}{2u_{m}^{2}}}\right)} \enum{tanh1}, \ee where \be t_{y} = \frac{1}{2} ln\left(\frac{1+y}{1-y}\right). \ee
nodes.section: Sequential saturation with the hyperbolic tangent
conclusions: will have a probability density function (pdf) given by
nodes.statement_short: Closed-form pdf of $\tanh(Y)$ for $Y \sim \mathcal{N}(0,u_m^2)$.

nodes.name: Sequential saturation with the hyperbolic tangent
nodes.statement: From the results in \cite{godfrey2009tanh}, we expect the activations to be (a) approximately normally distributed when $u_{m}$ is close to 0 and (b) bimodally distributed with local maximas near -1 and +1 when $u_{m}$ is close to 1. Accordingly, since $u_{m}^{2}$ is a decreasing function of $m$, we expect the activations from the shallower layers to be more saturated (i.e., more concentrated near -1 and +1), and the saturation in the activations to reduce as we go to the deeper layers in the network.
nodes.section: Sequential saturation with the hyperbolic tangent
assumptions: since $u_{m}^{2}$ is a decreasing function of $m$
conclusions: we expect the activations from the shallower layers to be more saturated (i.e., more concentrated near -1 and +1), and the saturation in the activations to reduce as we go to the deeper layers in the network
nodes.statement_short: Shallower tanh layers are more saturated; saturation decreases with depth.

nodes.name: Initialization for the sigmoid activation
nodes.statement: For the sigmoid activation defined as \be g(x) = \frac{1}{1 + \mbox{e}^{-x}} \ee we have $g(0) = 0.5$, $g'(0) = 1/4$. Plugging these values in \eref{in208} yields \be v \approx \frac{3.6}{\sqrt{N}}, \enum{relur} \ee
nodes.statement_short: For the sigmoid, the general formula gives $v \approx 3.6/\sqrt{N}$.

nodes.name: CIFAR-10 sigmoid convergence experiment
nodes.statement: First, I train the neural network with the {\it{Xavier initialization}} for 10 iterations and compute the top 5 accuracy on the validation dataset for each iteration. Next, I repeat the process using the initialization stated in \eref{relur}. A comparison of the validation accuracies for the 2 cases is provided in Figure \ref{fig:conv}, which shows that the convergence appears to stall with the {\it{Xavier initialization}}, but proceeds rapidly with the initialization proposed in \eref{relur}.
nodes.statement_short: On CIFAR-10, the sigmoid init $3.6/\sqrt{N}$ converges while Xavier stalls.

nodes.name: Derivation of the He initialization for RELU
nodes.statement: Since the RELU activation is not differentiable at 0, the results from \erefs{in205}{in207} cannot be used to compute the optimal value of $v^{2}$. To proceed, I use proposition 2 and \eref{in201} which state that for the first iteration, $ y_{m}(i) \sim {\cal{N}}(0,u_{m}^{2})$. We are interested in in the mean and variance of $x_{m+1}(i) = \mbox{max}(0,y_{m}(i))$. The mean will be given by \be \mu_{m+1} = E(y_{m}(i){\bf{I}}(y_{m}(i)>0)) = \frac{1}{{u_{m}\sqrt{2\pi}}}\int_{0}^{\infty} x \mbox{e}^{-\frac{x^{2}}{2u_{m}^{2}}}dx = \frac{u_{m}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{0}^{\infty}\mbox{e}^{-t}dt = \frac{u_{m}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}. \enum{relu1} \ee Similarly, \be E(x_{m+1}(i)^{2}) = \frac{1}{{u_{m}\sqrt{2\pi}}}\int_{0}^{\infty} x^{2} \mbox{e}^{-\frac{x^{2}}{2u_{m}^{2}}}dx = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right) \frac{1}{{u\sqrt{2\pi}}} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x^{2} \mbox{e}^{-\frac{x^{2}}{2u^{2}}}dx = \frac{u_{m}^{2}}{2}. \enum{relu2} \ee Using \eref{relu1} and \eref{relu2}, \be s_{m+1}^{2} = E(x_{m+1}(i)^{2}) - \mu_{m+1}^{2} = \frac{u_{m}^{2}}{2} - \frac{u_{m}^{2}}{2\pi} \approx 0.34u_{m}^{2}. \enum{relu3} \ee For the variance to be maintained at each iteration, we require $s_{m+1}^{2} \approx 1$ which yields \be u_{m}^{2} \approx 3. \enum{relu301} \ee Plugging \eref{relu301} in \eref{relu1} yields $\mu_{m+1} \approx 0.7$. By the symmetry of the problem during the first iteration, we expect $\mu_{m+1} \approx \mu_{m} ... \approx \mu_{2} \approx 0.7$. Using this result in \eref{in204} yields \be 3 = Nv^{2}(1+ 0.49) \ee
nodes.statement_short: Compute the mean and variance of a rectified Gaussian and impose unit variance at each layer.

nodes.name: He initialization for RELU
nodes.statement: \be v^{2}\approx 2/N, \ee which is consistent with that obtained by \cite{he2015delving}.
assumptions: For the variance to be maintained at each iteration, we require $s_{m+1}^{2} \approx 1$
nodes.statement_short: For RELU, variance preservation requires $v^2 \approx 2/N$ (the He initialization).

nodes.name: Derivation of RELU moments under Xavier initialization
nodes.statement: To understand why this happens, I compute the central moments of $x_{m+1}$ in terms of the central moments of $x_{m}$ when $v^{2} = 1/N$. From \eref{in204} we have \be u_{m}^{2} = s_{m}^{2} + \mu_{m}^{2}. \enum{r01} \ee Plugging results from \eref{r01} into \eref{relu1} yields the recursion \be \mu_{m+1}^{2} = \frac{1}{2\pi}(s_{m}^{2} + \mu_{m}^{2}) \approx 0.16(s_{m}^{2} + \mu_{m}^{2}). \enum{r02} \ee Similarly, plugging results from \eref{r01} and \eref{r02} in \eref{relu3} yields \be s_{m+1}^{2} \approx 0.34(s_{m}^{2} + \mu_{m}^{2}). \enum{relu5} \ee Simple manipulations of equations \erefs{r01}{relu5} gives
nodes.section: To converge or not to converge, that is the question.
nodes.statement_short: Substitute $v^2=1/N$ into the RELU moment formulas to get linear recursions for $\mu_m^2$, $s_m^2$.

nodes.name: Exponential variance decay of RELU with Xavier initialization
nodes.statement: \be \mu_{m}^{2} \approx 0.16 \times (0.51)^{m-1} \enum{relu603} \ee and \be s_{m}^{2} \approx 0.34 \times (0.51)^{m-1}. \enum{relu602} \ee for all $m \geq 1$.
nodes.section: To converge or not to converge, that is the question.
nodes.statement_short: With RELU and $v^2=1/N$, $\mu_m^2$ and $s_m^2$ decay like $(0.51)^{m-1}$.

nodes.name: Agreement with CS231n simulations
nodes.statement: These approximations are remarkably accurate, as is demonstrated by comparisons with the simulation experiments described in Figure \ref{fig:cs231ncomp}.
nodes.section: To converge or not to converge, that is the question.

nodes.name: Xavier initialization degrades with depth under RELU
nodes.statement: Equation \eref{relu602} shows that the variance of the inputs to the deeper layers is exponentially smaller than the variance of the inputs to the shallower layer. Therefore, the deeper the neural network, the worse the performance of the {\it{Xavier Initialization}} will be. From \eref{relu602}, $s_{22}^{2} \approx 1.62 \times 10^{-7}$ and $s_{30}^{2} \approx 6.33 \times 10^{-10}$. Thus the variance in the input to the $30^{th}$ layer will be $(0.51)^{8} = 3 \times 10^{-3}$ times smaller than the variance to the $22^{nd}$ layer, and explains the possible reason why the 30 layer neural network described in \cite{he2015delving} converges, but the 22 layer neural network does not.
nodes.section: To converge or not to converge, that is the question.
conclusions: the variance of the inputs to the deeper layers is exponentially smaller than the variance of the inputs to the shallower layer
the deeper the neural network, the worse the performance of the {\it{Xavier Initialization}} will be
nodes.statement_short: Input variance shrinks exponentially with depth, explaining the convergence gap between the 22- and 30-layer RELU networks.

nodes.name: Express inputs via earlier weights
nodes.statement: Using the recursions in \eref{in1} and \eref{in2}, $x_{m}(k)$ can be expressed as some non-linear function of the weights in the first $m-1$ layers, and the inputs to the first layer.
nodes.statement_short: Unroll the recursions: $x_m(k)$ is a function of earlier weights and first-layer inputs.

nodes.name: Independence of layer-$m$ weights
nodes.statement: Since the weights in the $m^{th}$ layer are independent of the inputs to the first layer and the weights in all other layers, the weights in the $m^{th}$ layer will also be independent of any non-linear function of these quantities. Therefore, $W_{m}(i,j)$ is independent of $x_{m}(k)$ for all values of $i, j$ and $k$.
nodes.statement_short: Functions of independent quantities stay independent of the layer-$m$ weights.

nodes.name: Extend to products
nodes.statement: Furthermore, since $W_{m}(i,j)$ is independent of $x_{m}(k)$ and $x_{m}(l)$, $W_{m}(i,j)$ will also be independent of $x_{m}(k)x_{m}(l)$\qedsymbol
nodes.statement_short: Independence extends to products $x_m(k)x_m(l)$.

nodes.name: Variance equals second moment
nodes.statement: Therefore, $u_{m}^{2} = Var(y_{m}(i)) = E\left(y_{m}(i)^{2}\right) - \left(E(y_{m}(i))\right)^{2} = E\left(y_{m}(i)^{2}\right)$.
nodes.statement_short: Zero mean makes the variance equal to the second moment.

nodes.name: Expand the square
nodes.statement: Using \eref{in1}, \be \begin{split} u_{m}^{2} &= E\left(\sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N}{\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)x_{m}(j)\right)^{2} \\ &= \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N} E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)^{2}x_{m}(j)^{2}\right) + 2\sum E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)x_{m}(j){\bf{W}}_{m}(k,l)x_{m}(l)\right). \\ \enum{in203} \end{split} \ee
nodes.statement_short: Expand $E(y_m^2)$ into diagonal and cross terms.

nodes.name: Cross terms vanish
nodes.statement: From proposition 1, ${\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)$ and ${\bf{W}}_{m}(k,l)$ will (a) be independent of each other, and (b) be independent of $x_{m}(j)x_{m}(l)$. Using these results, along with the fact that $E({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)) = 0 $ gives \newline \be E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)x_{m}(j){\bf{W}}_{m}(k,l)x_{m}(l)\right) = E({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j))E({\bf{W}}_{m}(k,l))E(x_{m}(j)x_{m}(l)) = 0. \enum{in2041} \ee
nodes.statement_short: Proposition 1 and zero-mean weights kill the cross terms.

nodes.name: Combine
nodes.statement: Plugging \eref{in2041} into \eref{in203} gives
nodes.statement_short: Substitute the vanishing cross terms.

nodes.name: Zero-mean summands
nodes.statement: For the first iteration, note that $E(p_{ij}) = E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)x_{m}(j)\right) = E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)\right)E\left(x_{m}(j)\right) = 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Each $p_{ij}$ has mean zero.

nodes.name: Uncorrelated summands
nodes.statement: Furthermore, for $j \neq k$, \be \begin{split} Cov(p_{ij},p_{ik})&= E(p_{ij}p_{ik}) - E(p_{ij})E(p_{ik}) \\ &= E(p_{ij}p_{ik}) \\ &= E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)x_{m}(j){\bf{W}}_{m}(i,k)x_{m}(k)\right) = 0,\\ \end{split} \ee where the last equality follows from \eref{in2041}.
nodes.statement_short: The $p_{ij}$ are uncorrelated by the cross-term identity.

nodes.name: Central Limit Theorem
nodes.statement: This implies that $p_{i1}$, $p_{i2}$ ... $p_{iN}$ are independent and identically distributed random variables. Therefore by the Central Limit Theorem, we expect $y_{m}(i) = \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N} p_{ij}$ to converge to a normal distribution when $N$ is large \cite{lehmann2004elements}.
nodes.statement_short: Treat the $p_{ij}$ as i.i.d. and apply the CLT.

nodes.name: Dependent case
nodes.statement: Even when $p_{i1}$, $p_{i2}$ ... $p_{iN}$ are dependent and not identically distributed, the conditions required to ensure that $y_{m}(i) = \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N} p_{ij}$ converges to a normal distribution are weak (for a list of all the conditions, see Theorem 2.8.2 in \cite{lehmann2004elements}).
nodes.statement_short: Weak CLT conditions cover the dependent, non-identical case.

nodes.name: Conclude approximate normality
nodes.statement: Thus, $y_{m}(i)$ is expected to to be approximately normally distributed during most iterations. \qedsymbol
nodes.statement_short: $y_m(i)$ is approximately normal.

nodes.name: Mean of next-layer inputs
nodes.statement: Taking the expectation in \eref{in205} gives \be \mu_{m+1} = E(x_{m+1}(i)) \approx g(0). \enum{in206} \ee
nodes.statement_short: Expectation of the linearization gives $\mu_{m+1} \approx g(0)$.

nodes.name: Mean decoupled from previous moments
nodes.statement: This equation suggests that the expected value of the inputs to the $(m+1)^{th}$ layer has little dependence on the moments of the inputs to the ${m}^{th}$ layer.
nodes.statement_short: The next-layer mean does not depend on previous moments.

nodes.name: Recursive application
nodes.statement: Using this result recursively suggests that for all layers (barring the first), \be \mu_{j} = g(0) \mbox{ for all } j\geq 1 \enum{in2061}. \ee
nodes.statement_short: Apply recursively: $\mu_j = g(0)$ for all layers.

nodes.name: Variance recursion
nodes.statement: Using \eref{in204} and \eref{in2061}, the variance of $x_{m+1}(i)$ can be computed from \eref{in205} as \be \begin{split} s_{m+1}^{2} = Var(x_{m+1}(i)) &\approx (g'(0))^{2} Var(y_{m}(i)) \\ &= N(g'(0))^{2}v^{2}(s_{m}^{2} + \mu_{m}^{2}) \\ &= N(g'(0))^{2}v^{2}(s_{m}^{2} + g(0)^{2}) . \enum{in207} \end{split} \ee
nodes.statement_short: Combine with the pre-activation variance formula to get $s_{m+1}^2$.

nodes.name: Glorot-Bengio uniform initialization
nodes.statement: To explain their finding, I begin by noting that in \cite{glorot2010understanding}, the authors initialize the weights using samples from a uniform distribution $\left(U[-1/\sqrt{N},1/\sqrt{N}]\right)$ having a variance of $1/3N$.
nodes.statement_short: Recall that Glorot-Bengio use a uniform init with variance $1/3N$.
nodes.section: Sequential saturation with the hyperbolic tangent

nodes.name: Shrinking variance recursion
nodes.statement: Therefore, from \eref{in2061} and \eref{in207}, with $g(0) = 0$ and $g'(0) = 1$, we have $\mu_{m} = 0$ and \be s_{m+1}^{2} = \frac{1}{3}s_{m}^{2} < s_{m}^{2} \ee \enum{seq1} respectively.
nodes.statement_short: Plug into the recursion: $s_{m+1}^2 = s_m^2/3$.
nodes.section: Sequential saturation with the hyperbolic tangent

nodes.name: Decreasing pre-activation variance
nodes.statement: From \eref{in204}, this implies that $u_{m+1}^{2}<u_{m}^{2}$ for all $m$ (i.e., $u_{m}^{2}$ is a decreasing function of $m$).
nodes.statement_short: Hence $u_m^2$ decreases in $m$.
nodes.section: Sequential saturation with the hyperbolic tangent

nodes.name: Gaussian pre-activations
nodes.statement: Furthermore from proposition 2, $y_{m}(i) \sim {\cal{N}}(0,u_{m}^{2})$. Therefore, $x_{m+1}(i)$ will be the tanh transformation of a normal random variable.
nodes.statement_short: By Proposition 2, activations are tanh of a Gaussian.
nodes.section: Sequential saturation with the hyperbolic tangent

nodes.name: Tanh-Gaussian density
nodes.statement: Using results from \cite{godfrey2009tanh}, $x_{m+1}(i) = \mbox{tanh}(y_{m}(i))$ will have a probability density function (pdf) given by \be f(y) = \frac{1}{1-y^{2}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi u_{m}^{2}}}\mbox{e}^{\left({-\frac{t_{y}^{2}}{2u_{m}^{2}}}\right)} \enum{tanh1}, \ee where \be t_{y} = \frac{1}{2} ln\left(\frac{1+y}{1-y}\right). \ee
nodes.statement_short: Invoke Godfrey's pdf of tanh of a Gaussian.
nodes.section: Sequential saturation with the hyperbolic tangent

nodes.name: Comparison with simulations
nodes.statement: Plots of this pdf for different values of $u_{m}$ (provided in Figure \ref{fig:tanh}) produce trends similar to those observed by the simulation studies of \cite{glorot2010understanding} (figure 4 in their paper). A comparison of Figure \ref{fig:tanh} and figure 4 of \cite{glorot2010understanding} suggests that $u_{m}^{2}$ is a decreasing function of $m$, as is expected.
nodes.statement_short: The plotted pdfs match Glorot-Bengio's figure 4.
nodes.section: Sequential saturation with the hyperbolic tangent

nodes.name: Taylor approach unavailable
nodes.statement: Since the RELU activation is not differentiable at 0, the results from \erefs{in205}{in207} cannot be used to compute the optimal value of $v^{2}$.
nodes.statement_short: Linearization fails for RELU.

nodes.name: Gaussian pre-activations
nodes.statement: To proceed, I use proposition 2 and \eref{in201} which state that for the first iteration, $ y_{m}(i) \sim {\cal{N}}(0,u_{m}^{2})$.
nodes.statement_short: Use Proposition 2 and zero mean: $y_m \sim \mathcal{N}(0,u_m^2)$.

nodes.name: Mean of rectified Gaussian
nodes.statement: We are interested in in the mean and variance of $x_{m+1}(i) = \mbox{max}(0,y_{m}(i))$. The mean will be given by \be \mu_{m+1} = E(y_{m}(i){\bf{I}}(y_{m}(i)>0)) = \frac{1}{{u_{m}\sqrt{2\pi}}}\int_{0}^{\infty} x \mbox{e}^{-\frac{x^{2}}{2u_{m}^{2}}}dx = \frac{u_{m}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{0}^{\infty}\mbox{e}^{-t}dt = \frac{u_{m}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}. \enum{relu1} \ee
nodes.statement_short: Compute $\mu_{m+1} = u_m/\sqrt{2\pi}$.

nodes.name: Second moment of rectified Gaussian
nodes.statement: Similarly, \be E(x_{m+1}(i)^{2}) = \frac{1}{{u_{m}\sqrt{2\pi}}}\int_{0}^{\infty} x^{2} \mbox{e}^{-\frac{x^{2}}{2u_{m}^{2}}}dx = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right) \frac{1}{{u\sqrt{2\pi}}} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x^{2} \mbox{e}^{-\frac{x^{2}}{2u^{2}}}dx = \frac{u_{m}^{2}}{2}. \enum{relu2} \ee
nodes.statement_short: Compute $E(x_{m+1}^2) = u_m^2/2$.

nodes.name: Variance of rectified Gaussian
nodes.statement: Using \eref{relu1} and \eref{relu2}, \be s_{m+1}^{2} = E(x_{m+1}(i)^{2}) - \mu_{m+1}^{2} = \frac{u_{m}^{2}}{2} - \frac{u_{m}^{2}}{2\pi} \approx 0.34u_{m}^{2}. \enum{relu3} \ee
nodes.statement_short: Variance $s_{m+1}^2 \approx 0.34 u_m^2$.

nodes.name: Impose unit variance
nodes.statement: For the variance to be maintained at each iteration, we require $s_{m+1}^{2} \approx 1$ which yields \be u_{m}^{2} \approx 3. \enum{relu301} \ee
nodes.statement_short: Unit variance requires $u_m^2 \approx 3$.

nodes.name: Mean across layers
nodes.statement: Plugging \eref{relu301} in \eref{relu1} yields $\mu_{m+1} \approx 0.7$. By the symmetry of the problem during the first iteration, we expect $\mu_{m+1} \approx \mu_{m} ... \approx \mu_{2} \approx 0.7$.
nodes.statement_short: Hence $\mu \approx 0.7$ in every layer by symmetry.

nodes.name: Solve for $v^2$
nodes.statement: Using this result in \eref{in204} yields \be 3 = Nv^{2}(1+ 0.49) \ee
nodes.statement_short: Plug into the variance formula: $3 = N v^2 (1.49)$.

nodes.name: Set Xavier variance
nodes.statement: To understand why this happens, I compute the central moments of $x_{m+1}$ in terms of the central moments of $x_{m}$ when $v^{2} = 1/N$.
nodes.statement_short: Track the RELU moments when $v^2 = 1/N$.
nodes.section: To converge or not to converge, that is the question.

nodes.name: Pre-activation variance
nodes.statement: From \eref{in204} we have \be u_{m}^{2} = s_{m}^{2} + \mu_{m}^{2}. \enum{r01} \ee
nodes.section: To converge or not to converge, that is the question.

nodes.name: Mean recursion
nodes.statement: Plugging results from \eref{r01} into \eref{relu1} yields the recursion \be \mu_{m+1}^{2} = \frac{1}{2\pi}(s_{m}^{2} + \mu_{m}^{2}) \approx 0.16(s_{m}^{2} + \mu_{m}^{2}). \enum{r02} \ee
nodes.statement_short: Recursion for $\mu_{m+1}^2$.
nodes.section: To converge or not to converge, that is the question.

nodes.name: Variance recursion
nodes.statement: Similarly, plugging results from \eref{r01} and \eref{r02} in \eref{relu3} yields \be s_{m+1}^{2} \approx 0.34(s_{m}^{2} + \mu_{m}^{2}). \enum{relu5} \ee
nodes.statement_short: Recursion for $s_{m+1}^2$.
